title: Product Problem Formulation & Baselines
summary: Turn an ambiguous request into a decision, prediction unit, constraints, and the simplest credible baseline.
learningObjective: Decide whether ML is justified before selecting a model family.
scenario: A fraud team asks for AI to prioritize a review queue, but simple rules may already meet the first release's capacity and harm constraints.
mentalModel: Define the product action first; the model is only one possible way to support it.
interviewImpact: A precise decision unit and baseline keep the rest of the design measurable and prevent architecture-by-buzzword.
solves: Misalignment between model output and product value.
useWhen: At the start of every ML system discussion.
tradeoff: A tractable proxy target may not perfectly represent the product goal.
commonMistake: Starting with a model family instead of a decision and baseline.
mechanism: Name the user, stakeholder, decision, prediction unit, action, and reversible fallback.
Compare rules, a domain algorithm, and a simple model against latency, freshness, scale, and harm constraints.
alternatives: Use deterministic policy when the decision is fully specified and stable.
Use human triage when examples are scarce and review capacity is the dominant constraint.
productConsequences: A baseline defines what useful improvement means and exposes when automation is unnecessary.
operationalConsequences: Every added learning component creates data, deployment, monitoring, and rollback ownership.
failureModes: The prediction target is easy to label but unrelated to the desired action.
The model adds latency while producing no decision improvement over rules.
workedExample: Start with rules that route high-value, high-velocity transactions to review.
Add a scorer only after measuring unresolved queue ordering and label maturity.

exercise.prompt: Choose rules, a simple model, or richer ML for a 200-case daily review queue with stable policy and few confirmed outcomes.
exercise.expected: Prefer rules or a transparent simple model; identify what observation would justify richer ML.

interviewerProbes: What happens without ML?
Which requirement would change your baseline choice?

levelOverlays.entry: Define one decision and a defensible baseline.
levelOverlays.mid: Connect the baseline to data availability, serving, and fallback.
levelOverlays.senior: Challenge the ML premise and define organizational ownership for evolution.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML emphasizes integration; MLE balances the lifecycle; Applied Scientist deepens objective validity.

riskCallout: Automation can amplify a bad policy; keep review and appeal paths proportionate to harm.
decisionTrigger: What measured baseline gap, workload, or harm pattern would justify introducing ML?

title: Objectives, Metrics & Guardrails
summary: Connect business and user outcomes to task metrics without mistaking a proxy for the product goal.
learningObjective: Build a layered metric map with task-specific quality and operational guardrails.
scenario: A search team improves click-through while successful task completion falls and complaint rate rises.
mentalModel: A metric is a decision instrument, not the objective itself.
interviewImpact: Metrics determine labels, evaluation, experimentation, thresholding, and rollback signals.
solves: Proxy optimization that improves a model number while harming the product.
useWhen: Before dataset or architecture choices and again before launch.
tradeoff: Closer-to-value outcomes are often delayed, noisy, or expensive to measure.
commonMistake: Using accuracy or click-through as a universal objective.
mechanism: Map business outcome to user outcome, task metric, diagnostic slices, and guardrails.
State where the optimization target is only a proxy and how delayed outcomes validate it.
alternatives: Use a constraint or policy rule when a harmful outcome must not be traded away.
Use a metric set rather than a weighted scalar when stakeholders cannot justify exchange rates.
productConsequences: The wrong proxy can reward clickbait, concentration, or needless interventions.
operationalConsequences: Guardrails create monitoring, experiment-stop, and rollback requirements.
failureModes: One average hides a failing cohort.
Offline improvement is assumed to imply causal product improvement.
workedExample: Search uses task completion as a user outcome, NDCG@K as ranking quality, and latency, zero-result rate, and complaints as guardrails.
An online experiment tests whether offline gains transfer without violating those guardrails.

exercise.prompt: Create a metric map for search where users click more but reformulate more often.
exercise.expected: Separate clicks from successful task completion and add reformulation, zero-result, latency, and complaint diagnostics.

interviewerProbes: Which metric is causal evidence?
What slice or guardrail could reverse the launch decision?

levelOverlays.entry: Choose a task-appropriate metric and one guardrail.
levelOverlays.mid: Connect offline, online, slice, and operational measures.
levelOverlays.senior: Explain proxy conflict, capacity constraints, and long-term effects.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist deepens measurement validity; SWE-ML owns reliable instrumentation.

riskCallout: Metrics encode product values; review subgroup errors and avoid turning protected traits into casual optimization inputs.
decisionTrigger: Which user outcome or guardrail movement would make an offline gain unacceptable?

title: Data Collection, Logging & Data Quality
summary: Design observable events, exposures, schemas, timestamps, consent, quality checks, and lineage before training.
learningObjective: Trace a product event into a trustworthy training example.
scenario: A recommender records clicks but not which items were shown, so missing interactions cannot be interpreted as negatives.
mentalModel: A training row is only as trustworthy as the events and context that produced it.
interviewImpact: Logging choices determine label validity, counterfactual gaps, debugging, and privacy scope.
solves: Training data that cannot explain what the product exposed or when it happened.
useWhen: Before labels, feature joins, or offline evaluation.
tradeoff: Richer observability improves diagnosis but raises cost, retention, and privacy exposure.
commonMistake: Saying collect user data without defining exposure, identity, time, or consent.
mechanism: Log decisions, eligible candidates, exposures, positions, context, outcomes, and event time with versioned contracts.
Validate schema, ranges, missingness, volume, freshness, duplicates, and late arrival before examples publish.
alternatives: Sample events when full fidelity is too costly, but preserve known inclusion probabilities.
Aggregate at source when raw events add no justified value and increase privacy risk.
productConsequences: Missing exposure data makes ranking and recommendation feedback ambiguous.
operationalConsequences: Schema owners, retention policy, replay, backfill, and quality alerts become production dependencies.
failureModes: Client versions emit incompatible event meanings.
Late or duplicated events silently corrupt labels and aggregates.
workedExample: A recommendation impression logs request, user/session, eligible set, shown items, positions, policy version, and timestamp.
Clicks and later outcomes join only after validation and a defined maturation window.

exercise.prompt: Design the minimum event set needed to learn from a five-item recommendation carousel.
exercise.expected: Include eligibility, exposure and position, not only interactions; define identifiers, time, version, and consent.

interviewerProbes: How do you detect a broken mobile logger?
What data can you avoid retaining?

levelOverlays.entry: Name the core events and identifiers.
levelOverlays.mid: Add contracts, validation, lateness, and lineage.
levelOverlays.senior: Define ownership, consent, repair, backfill, and policy evolution.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML emphasizes ingestion reliability; MLE connects it to examples and monitoring.

riskCallout: Collect only justified signals, enforce access and retention, and avoid placing private attempt content in analytics.
decisionTrigger: Which missing event or quality observation would invalidate the training set?

title: Labels, Ground Truth & Label Delay
summary: Turn observable outcomes into labels while making delay, noise, dispute, and proxy risk explicit.
learningObjective: Define positive, negative, unknown, and mutable label states with a maturation policy.
scenario: A purchase that occurs a day after an ad click is prematurely labeled negative at training time.
mentalModel: A label is an operational definition of evidence, not objective truth.
interviewImpact: Label design changes dataset windows, retraining cadence, evaluation, review, and appeals.
solves: Noisy or premature targets that teach the model the wrong behavior.
useWhen: Whenever outcomes are delayed, disputed, implicit, or reviewed by people.
tradeoff: Waiting improves label maturity but makes learning less fresh.
commonMistake: Treating unobserved behavior as a confirmed negative.
mechanism: Define the observation window and states such as pending, positive, confirmed negative, reversed, and disputed.
Record label source, policy version, reviewer context, and correction history.
alternatives: Use weak supervision when verified outcomes are scarce, and measure disagreement.
Use positive-unlabeled framing when non-events are not reliable negatives.
productConsequences: Premature negatives bias delayed-conversion and long-horizon systems.
operationalConsequences: Mutable labels require recomputation, lineage, adjudication, and backfill controls.
failureModes: Reviewer decisions are treated as infallible ground truth.
Label policy changes without versioning historical examples.
workedExample: A chargeback label remains pending through the dispute window.
Reversals update the label record and future datasets without silently rewriting prior experiments.

exercise.prompt: Define label states for fraud where chargebacks arrive weeks later and some are reversed.
exercise.expected: Use pending/mature/reversed states, time-aware training eligibility, and reviewer or dispute provenance.

interviewerProbes: When does a negative become trustworthy?
How do corrections reach old datasets?

levelOverlays.entry: Define a clear positive and negative.
levelOverlays.mid: Handle maturation, noise, and correction.
levelOverlays.senior: Design label operations, adjudication, auditability, and policy migrations.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist owns target validity; MLE owns operational label state.

riskCallout: Human labels may reflect inconsistent policy or bias; preserve appeal, review quality, and provenance.
decisionTrigger: What delay, disagreement, or reversal rate would change the label policy?

title: Dataset Construction, Splits & Leakage
summary: Build evaluation data that resembles future deployment and blocks information from leaking backward.
learningObjective: Choose temporal, entity, or group splits and perform point-in-time joins.
scenario: A demand forecast looks excellent under a random split because future seasonal observations leak into training.
mentalModel: Train as if you were standing at the historical decision time.
interviewImpact: The split is part of the system design because it defines what offline evidence means.
solves: Optimistic evaluation caused by future information, duplicate entities, or unrealistic prevalence.
useWhen: Before model comparison or backtesting.
tradeoff: Realistic splits reduce usable training data and often produce noisier estimates.
commonMistake: Randomly splitting temporal or entity-correlated examples.
mechanism: Choose the unit that must not cross splits and set a historical cutoff for every feature and label.
Deduplicate, preserve realistic prevalence, document negative sampling, and run leakage audits.
alternatives: Use rolling-origin backtests for forecasting and changing environments.
Use group holdouts when deployment must generalize to unseen users, devices, or organizations.
productConsequences: Leakage creates launch regressions despite impressive offline results.
operationalConsequences: Point-in-time datasets require immutable snapshots, time-aware joins, and reproducible backfills.
failureModes: The same entity appears in train and test without justification.
A feature is computed after the decision or from the eventual label.
workedExample: Forecasting trains on weeks before a cutoff and validates on the next horizon.
The process rolls forward across several cutoffs to expose seasonal instability.

exercise.prompt: Find leakage in a churn model using current account status to predict last month's churn.
exercise.expected: Reconstruct status as of the historical decision time and split by time or account as deployment requires.

interviewerProbes: What is the split unit?
How do you prove every feature existed at prediction time?

levelOverlays.mid: Use point-in-time joins and deployment-shaped splits.
levelOverlays.senior: Design backtesting, replay, audit, and migration strategy.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML builds reliable dataset tooling; Applied Scientist defends evaluation validity.

riskCallout: Dataset construction can overrepresent highly observed users and erase groups with sparse data; inspect coverage by slice.
decisionTrigger: Which deployment difference would make this split invalid?

title: Features & Feature Engineering
summary: Choose representations that exist at decision time with explicit freshness, ownership, and serving cost.
learningObjective: Turn raw signals into available, stable, and useful decision-time features.
scenario: An ETA model uses traffic aggregates refreshed every hour for a decision that must react within minutes.
mentalModel: A feature is a timed dependency with semantics, not just a column.
interviewImpact: Feature availability and cost shape both the training graph and hot serving path.
solves: Useful raw signals that need stable transformations and prediction-time availability.
useWhen: After labels and point-in-time constraints are clear.
tradeoff: Fresh and expressive features often cost more to compute and serve reliably.
commonMistake: Listing features without freshness, missing-value, or availability policy.
mechanism: Classify features as static, dynamic, or request context and set windows, time semantics, and owners.
Define missing, stale, and fallback behavior before adding them to the serving contract.
alternatives: Use raw or model-learned representations when manual features add brittle maintenance.
Drop a feature whose incremental quality does not justify latency, privacy, or ownership cost.
productConsequences: Fresh context can improve decisions but stale context can be worse than a simpler baseline.
operationalConsequences: Every online feature adds compute, storage, serving, validation, and incident surface.
failureModes: Training sees a feature that online serving cannot reproduce.
Default values hide an upstream outage.
workedExample: ETA starts with route distance and historical duration, then adds traffic and location context only within a latency budget.
Each feature has an event-time window, freshness threshold, and fallback.

exercise.prompt: Budget features for a 60 ms fraud decision where identity lookup costs 25 ms and velocity costs 20 ms.
exercise.expected: Allocate explicit feature latency, parallelize safe reads, cache stable attributes, and specify timeout fallback.

interviewerProbes: What exists at prediction time?
What happens when this feature is stale or missing?

levelOverlays.mid: Add freshness, cost, and skew controls.
levelOverlays.senior: Define feature ownership, deprecation, privacy, and incident policy.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML emphasizes serving contracts; Applied Scientist emphasizes signal validity.

riskCallout: Sensitive or proxy attributes require a justified purpose, access boundary, and outcome review.
decisionTrigger: What incremental quality gain would justify this feature's latency and ownership cost?

title: Embeddings & Learned Representations
summary: Use learned similarity while owning its training objective, index, refresh, filters, and version lifecycle.
learningObjective: Explain what an embedding represents and how it moves through retrieval and rollout.
scenario: Semantic search adds document embeddings but has no index refresh or permissions plan.
mentalModel: An embedding is a versioned representation optimized for a task—not meaning in a bottle.
interviewImpact: Representations introduce training objectives, negative selection, approximate retrieval, and coupled model/index deployment.
solves: Similarity and retrieval where sparse identifiers or lexical overlap are insufficient.
useWhen: When learned similarity earns measurable recall or generalization gains.
tradeoff: Dense representations improve recall but reduce transparency and add lifecycle coupling.
commonMistake: Saying use embeddings without defining objective, negatives, filters, or refresh.
mechanism: Train query/user and item/document representations against explicit positive and negative relationships.
Build a versioned index, apply eligibility and permissions, and measure candidate recall before ranking quality.
alternatives: Use lexical retrieval for exact terms, identifiers, and transparent fallback.
Use content or popularity baselines for cold-start entities.
productConsequences: Similarity quality shapes discovery, coverage, and cold-start behavior.
operationalConsequences: Encoder and index versions need compatible rollout, refresh, and rollback.
failureModes: The 2D demo is mistaken for literal production geometry.
A new encoder serves against an incompatible old index.
workedExample: Semantic search encodes documents offline and queries online, then retrieves approximate neighbors.
A lexical branch and permissions filter protect exact matches and access control.

exercise.prompt: Plan an encoder upgrade when re-embedding the corpus takes six hours.
exercise.expected: Build a parallel versioned index, shadow queries, compare recall and latency, then switch atomically with rollback.

interviewerProbes: What objective trained the representation?
How are model and index versions coordinated?

levelOverlays.mid: Cover negatives, recall, refresh, and filters.
levelOverlays.senior: Design version migration, cost, permission revocation, and multi-tenant isolation.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist deepens objectives; SWE-ML deepens indexing and rollout.

riskCallout: Representations can encode sensitive correlations; evaluate slices, access, retention, and misuse.
decisionTrigger: What recall gap or corpus property makes dense retrieval worth the lifecycle cost?

visual.title: Versioned representation path
visual.note: The visual is an illustration of higher-dimensional representations, not literal 2D geometry.

title: Class Imbalance, Sampling & Negative Examples
summary: Train and evaluate rare-event or huge-candidate problems without confusing sampled prevalence with reality.
learningObjective: Select weighting and negative sampling based on exposure and deployment prevalence.
scenario: A fraud detector reports 99.9% accuracy by predicting every rare positive as negative.
mentalModel: Sampling changes the data distribution; evaluation and calibration must know how.
interviewImpact: Negative construction changes what the model learns and what offline metrics mean.
solves: Learning when positives are rare or most candidate pairs are unobserved.
useWhen: For fraud, abuse, ads, recommendation, retrieval, and other sparse-outcome tasks.
tradeoff: Harder negatives improve discrimination but may overfocus training on a narrow boundary.
commonMistake: Using accuracy or easy random negatives without exposure context.
mechanism: Measure natural prevalence and distinguish exposed non-events from unknown candidates.
Choose weighting, under/oversampling, and hard negatives; correct evaluation for the sampled distribution.
alternatives: Use anomaly detection only when labeled positives are genuinely unavailable and validate operational usefulness.
Use rules for rare high-harm signatures with insufficient learning evidence.
productConsequences: Poor negative design produces irrelevant recommendations or missed rare harms.
operationalConsequences: Sampling policies must be versioned with datasets and monitored as inventory changes.
failureModes: Offline prevalence differs from production with no correction.
Unexposed items are labeled disliked.
workedExample: Fraud training weights rare positives and evaluates on natural prevalence.
Recommendation samples from eligible impressions plus hard near-misses, while treating unseen items as unknown.

exercise.prompt: Compare 1:1 sampled fraud evaluation with a production prevalence of 0.2%.
exercise.expected: Reject raw sampled accuracy or calibration; evaluate on natural prevalence and precision-recall operating points.

interviewerProbes: Where did negatives come from?
Does evaluation preserve production prevalence?

levelOverlays.mid: Design exposure-aware negatives and evaluation.
levelOverlays.senior: Own sampling correction, exploration, reviewer capacity, and adversarial adaptation.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist deepens estimator effects; MLE owns pipeline versioning.

riskCallout: Sampling can erase rare subgroups or amplify enforcement bias; inspect inclusion and error rates by relevant slice.
decisionTrigger: What prevalence or hard-negative error would change the sampling strategy?

title: Offline Evaluation by ML Task
summary: Choose metrics and error analysis for classification, ranking, retrieval, regression, and forecasting.
learningObjective: Match the metric to the decision and expose errors hidden by an average.
scenario: Candidate retrieval and final ranking are both evaluated with one generic accuracy score.
mentalModel: Evaluate each stage on the failure it can actually cause.
interviewImpact: Task metrics gate model and architecture choices before expensive rollout.
solves: Metric bingo and averages that hide stage or cohort failures.
useWhen: For every offline acceptance and model comparison decision.
tradeoff: More slices and metrics improve diagnosis but raise false-discovery and governance burden.
commonMistake: Using one universal metric with no baseline, slices, or error taxonomy.
mechanism: Classification uses precision/recall and threshold-aware analysis; retrieval uses Recall@K or MRR; ranking uses NDCG; regression uses MAE/RMSE/quantiles; forecasting adds rolling backtests.
Compare against a credible baseline, inspect slices, and classify errors by operational consequence.
alternatives: Use human evaluation for qualities not captured by reliable labels, with a defined rubric and sampling plan.
Use simulation only when its assumptions are validated against real outcomes.
productConsequences: Stage-specific evaluation prevents a good ranker from hiding a weak retriever.
operationalConsequences: Evaluation datasets, baselines, and slice definitions need versioning and reproducible computation.
failureModes: An average hides a critical region or user cohort.
Confidence intervals and repeated comparisons are ignored.
workedExample: Search first checks candidate Recall@K, then NDCG@K for ordering, plus zero-result and permission failures.
An error review separates missing candidates, bad ranking, stale index, and unsafe results.

exercise.prompt: Choose metrics for candidate retrieval, final ranking, and ETA tail errors.
exercise.expected: Use Recall@K, NDCG@K or MRR, and MAE plus high-percentile or quantile error by relevant slice.

interviewerProbes: Which metric belongs to which stage?
What error taxonomy guides the next change?

levelOverlays.entry: Choose a task-appropriate metric and baseline.
levelOverlays.mid: Add slices and error taxonomy.
levelOverlays.senior: Handle uncertainty, metric conflicts, and evaluation governance.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist deepens statistical validity; SWE-ML ensures reproducible pipelines.

riskCallout: Aggregate quality can conceal harmful subgroup behavior; use context-relevant slices without promising a universal fairness formula.
decisionTrigger: Which error type or slice result would block deployment despite an average gain?

title: Calibration & Decision Thresholds
summary: Turn scores into allow, review, challenge, block, or abstain actions under cost and capacity limits.
learningObjective: Choose thresholds from consequences and queue capacity rather than a default score.
scenario: A fraud team uses 0.5 as a block threshold although scores are uncalibrated and reviewers can handle only 2,000 cases.
mentalModel: The model ranks or estimates; policy converts that output into an action.
interviewImpact: Thresholds connect evaluation to business costs, human review, fallback, and appeals.
solves: Operational decisions with asymmetric false-positive and false-negative costs.
useWhen: When scores drive bounded interventions or queues.
tradeoff: Higher recall usually increases false positives and review load.
commonMistake: Treating a raw score as a probability or selecting 0.5 by default.
mechanism: Measure calibration by slice, estimate action costs, and define allow/review/challenge/block bands.
Bind thresholds to capacity, escalation, abstention, and rollback policy.
alternatives: Use rank-and-capacity selection when calibrated probability is unnecessary.
Use deterministic policy for non-negotiable constraints.
productConsequences: Thresholds determine user friction, harm, and appeal volume.
operationalConsequences: Queue capacity and label delay can force threshold changes independent of model quality.
failureModes: A threshold overloads reviewers and delays high-risk cases.
Global calibration hides a failing slice.
workedExample: Low-risk transactions pass, medium scores trigger step-up, high scores enter review, and only extreme verified policy cases block.
Bands are tested against cost and capacity, then monitored after launch.

exercise.prompt: Set action bands when review capacity is 1% of traffic and false blocks are expensive.
exercise.expected: Reserve review for the highest-value uncertain band, add step-up or abstention, and avoid automatic block without sufficient precision.

interviewerProbes: Is the score calibrated?
How does reviewer capacity change the operating point?

levelOverlays.mid: Add calibration, capacity, and action bands.
levelOverlays.senior: Design policy governance, appeals, and adaptive thresholds without silent harm.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist validates estimates; SWE-ML builds policy and queue controls.

riskCallout: High-impact actions need review, audit, and appeal proportional to harm; a model score is not a legal conclusion.
decisionTrigger: What cost, prevalence, or reviewer capacity would move the threshold bands?

title: Training Pipelines, Reproducibility & Lineage
summary: Build repeatable, validated workflows that connect data, code, configuration, evaluation, and artifacts.
learningObjective: Design a rerunnable pipeline with explicit publish gates and lineage.
scenario: A notebook retrains a ranker, overwrites a mutable dataset, and publishes an artifact no one can reproduce.
mentalModel: A model artifact is the output of a versioned graph, not an isolated file.
interviewImpact: Pipeline design determines repeatability, safe backfills, failure recovery, and auditability.
solves: Ad hoc training that cannot be explained, retried, or rolled back.
useWhen: Once a learning workflow repeats or influences production decisions.
tradeoff: Stronger lineage and gates slow informal iteration but reduce costly ambiguity.
commonMistake: Treating orchestration as a sequence of boxes without idempotency or artifact identity.
mechanism: Version code, configuration, input snapshots, feature definitions, environment, evaluation, and output artifact.
Make stages idempotent, validate before publish, isolate backfills, and retain lineage from artifact to inputs.
alternatives: Keep a simple scripted pipeline when scale and team boundaries do not justify a platform.
Use event-driven training only when events represent real evidence, not every data fluctuation.
productConsequences: Reliable reruns shorten recovery from bad data or model regressions.
operationalConsequences: Retries, quotas, backfills, artifact retention, and partial failure need explicit behavior.
failureModes: A retry duplicates side effects or publishes twice.
Mutable inputs prevent reproducing a released artifact.
workedExample: A daily ranker validates schemas, builds point-in-time examples, trains, evaluates against baseline and slices, then registers only accepted artifacts.
A failed publish leaves the current production version untouched.

exercise.prompt: Trace the exact inputs needed to reproduce yesterday's model.
exercise.expected: Identify immutable data snapshot, code, config, feature definitions, environment, seed, evaluation, and artifact metadata.

interviewerProbes: Which stages are safe to retry?
What evidence blocks publication?

levelOverlays.mid: Add lineage, retries, validation, and backfills.
levelOverlays.senior: Address multi-tenant compute, governance, disaster recovery, and ownership.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML owns orchestration; MLE connects model and platform semantics.

riskCallout: Lineage should include consent and access policy versions where data use is sensitive.
decisionTrigger: What failure or audit question would the current lineage be unable to answer?

title: Feature Stores & Training-Serving Consistency
summary: Reuse historical and online features without point-in-time corruption, skew, or hidden stale behavior.
learningObjective: Decide whether a feature store is earned and define its correctness contract.
scenario: Fraud velocity features are accurate online but historical training joins use today's latest values.
mentalModel: A feature store is a temporal contract and delivery system, not a mandatory database.
interviewImpact: The design must connect historical retrieval, materialization, online reads, ownership, and fallback.
solves: Reusable features that need consistent historical and low-latency values.
useWhen: When multiple models share feature definitions and point-in-time or online consistency is costly to maintain manually.
tradeoff: Reuse and consistency add platform complexity, tenancy, and migration obligations.
commonMistake: Assuming every ML system needs a feature store or joining latest values into old examples.
mechanism: Register owned feature definitions with event timestamps, transformations, and freshness contracts.
Retrieve historical values point-in-time, materialize online values, compare skew, and define stale/missing fallback.
alternatives: Keep features inside one pipeline when reuse and online access are limited.
Precompute batch features when decision latency does not require an online store.
productConsequences: Consistent features reduce unexplained online quality loss.
operationalConsequences: Backfills, materialization lag, online availability, deprecation, and tenant isolation become platform concerns.
failureModes: Training reads future values.
An online materialization delay silently serves stale features.
workedExample: Fraud velocity definitions support historical point-in-time retrieval and minute-level online materialization.
A stale store falls back to safer static signals and records the degraded path.

exercise.prompt: Decide whether one batch forecasting model needs a feature store.
exercise.expected: Usually no; keep transformations versioned in the pipeline unless reuse, historical correctness, or serving needs justify a platform.

interviewerProbes: Why not keep this in the pipeline?
How do you detect and handle training-serving skew?

levelOverlays.mid: Cover point-in-time retrieval, materialization, and fallback.
levelOverlays.senior: Design tenancy, migration, backfill isolation, ownership, and deprecation.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML deepens control/data plane; MLE validates semantics and freshness.

riskCallout: Central reuse widens access; apply least privilege, retention, and documented intended use.
decisionTrigger: What reuse, latency, or correctness cost makes a shared feature platform worthwhile?

title: Batch, Streaming & Online Inference
summary: Choose when features and predictions are computed from freshness, scale, and decision latency.
learningObjective: Distinguish batch scoring, streaming updates, precomputation, online inference, and hybrid paths.
scenario: A demand forecast is forced through request-time inference even though decisions update once per day.
mentalModel: Compute no later—and no earlier—than the decision requires.
interviewImpact: Inference mode changes cost, availability, event-time correctness, caching, and fallback.
solves: Matching prediction freshness to the real product decision.
useWhen: After latency and freshness requirements are measurable.
tradeoff: Fresher computation increases hot-path cost and dependency risk.
commonMistake: Calling everything real time or ignoring late event semantics.
mechanism: Map decision deadline, feature freshness, traffic, compute cost, and cacheability.
Select batch, precomputed, streaming, online, or hybrid paths and define late-data behavior.
alternatives: Serve precomputed results when per-request context adds little value.
Use streaming aggregates plus a simple online policy instead of online model inference.
productConsequences: Unnecessary real-time paths add latency without user value.
operationalConsequences: Streaming introduces event time, late data, state recovery, and replay; online inference introduces saturation and availability concerns.
failureModes: A batch job misses its publish deadline with no stale-mode policy.
Late events corrupt streaming features.
workedExample: Demand forecasts run daily in batch.
Fraud uses streaming velocity features and online scoring; recommendation precomputes candidates and ranks with request context.

exercise.prompt: Choose a mode for hourly inventory recommendations with per-session context.
exercise.expected: Precompute inventory candidates and combine them with light online ranking; define stale candidate and feature fallback.

interviewerProbes: What is the freshness requirement?
Could this decision be precomputed?

levelOverlays.mid: Add streaming, hybrid design, and late-data behavior.
levelOverlays.senior: Address regional placement, replay, cost, and migration between modes.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML emphasizes data paths; MLE balances freshness and quality.

riskCallout: Faster decisions can reduce time for human review; align mode with action reversibility and harm.
decisionTrigger: What freshness or context requirement rules out precomputation?

title: Model Serving & Performance Engineering
summary: Build a prediction data plane with explicit latency, throughput, resource, quality, and cost budgets.
learningObjective: Allocate the full request budget and design saturation and fallback behavior.
scenario: An inference endpoint meets average latency but cold starts and queueing violate p99 during bursts.
mentalModel: Serving performance is a queueing and dependency problem around a model computation.
interviewImpact: A credible answer budgets preprocessing, features, network, inference, postprocessing, and overload.
solves: Reliable low-latency or high-throughput model execution.
useWhen: When inference is on a production path or expensive batch fleet.
tradeoff: Batching improves throughput but adds waiting latency; warm capacity improves tail latency but costs more.
commonMistake: Drawing an endpoint and ignoring p99, queueing, loading, saturation, or fallback.
mechanism: Budget network, features, preprocessing, queue, inference, and policy latency at p50 and p99.
Choose CPU/GPU pools, batching, model loading, autoscaling, admission, caching, and fallback by workload.
alternatives: Use a smaller model or precomputation when hot-path quality gain is marginal.
Route to a lightweight baseline under saturation.
productConsequences: Tail latency and timeouts directly change user-visible quality and availability.
operationalConsequences: Model size, runtime compatibility, warmup, GPU fragmentation, and queue depth drive cost and incident behavior.
failureModes: Autoscaling reacts after queues are already overloaded.
Fallback violates policy or produces incompatible outputs.
workedExample: Small latency-sensitive models run on warm CPU pools; heavy batchable models use GPU pools with bounded queues.
Admission control sends overload to a tested lightweight fallback.

exercise.prompt: Allocate a 120 ms p99 budget across features, network, queue, inference, and postprocessing.
exercise.expected: Set explicit sub-budgets, reserve headroom, bound queues, and name the degradation path.

interviewerProbes: What dominates p99?
What happens when every worker is busy?

levelOverlays.mid: Cover batching, autoscaling, loading, and saturation.
levelOverlays.senior: Design multi-model tenancy, regional failover, cost control, and runtime migration.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML deepens performance; MLE connects quality to serving constraints.

riskCallout: Overload must fail safely for high-impact decisions; do not silently replace a reviewed path with an unsafe prediction.
decisionTrigger: Which p99, throughput, or cost observation would force a smaller model or different compute path?

title: Model Registry, Deployment & Rollback
summary: Promote compatible artifacts through shadow, canary, staged rollout, and reversible production changes.
learningObjective: Separate artifact registration from deployment and define compatibility and rollback signals.
scenario: A new encoder is deployed while the old vector index remains active, corrupting retrieval quality.
mentalModel: A release is a compatible version set plus a traffic decision, not a model file copy.
interviewImpact: Deployment must account for artifact identity, schema, features, index, runtime, policy, and audit trail.
solves: Moving accepted models into production safely and reversibly.
useWhen: For every model or coupled index/policy release.
tradeoff: Parallel versions and staged traffic increase cost but reduce blast radius.
commonMistake: Confusing a registry with deployment or shadow traffic with user-visible canary traffic.
mechanism: Register immutable artifacts with lineage, compatibility metadata, evaluation, and approval.
Deploy dark or shadow for behavior checks, canary real traffic with guardrails, stage the ramp, and keep rollback-compatible state.
alternatives: Use blue/green when traffic splitting is unsuitable but parallel capacity is available.
Keep the current version when offline improvement does not justify migration risk.
productConsequences: Staged rollout limits user exposure to quality or latency regressions.
operationalConsequences: Rollback depends on schema, feature, index, runtime, and state compatibility—not only retained binaries.
failureModes: Shadow results are mistaken for causal product evidence.
Rollback restores code but not a compatible index or schema.
workedExample: Encoder v2 builds index v2, shadows queries, then receives a small canary share while recall, latency, and guardrails are compared.
A routing switch returns traffic to the v1 pair if any block condition fires.

exercise.prompt: Order shadow, canary, experiment, promotion, and rollback for a coupled model/index release.
exercise.expected: Validate compatibility offline, shadow without impact, canary real traffic, experiment if causal impact matters, then promote with a tested paired rollback.

interviewerProbes: What exactly is versioned together?
Which signal triggers rollback and how fast?

levelOverlays.mid: Distinguish shadow, canary, and experiment.
levelOverlays.senior: Design multi-region migration, compatibility windows, governance, and incident ownership.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML owns rollout mechanics; Applied Scientist owns acceptance evidence.

riskCallout: Audit high-impact policy/model version changes and preserve a safe human or deterministic fallback.
decisionTrigger: Which compatibility or guardrail result blocks the next traffic step?

title: Online Experimentation & Causal Validation
summary: Test product impact with a valid hypothesis, randomization unit, exposure model, guardrails, and analysis plan.
learningObjective: Know when an online experiment is appropriate and what can invalidate it.
scenario: A feed test randomizes requests even though users appear repeatedly and creators influence both treatment groups.
mentalModel: An experiment is a causal design with integrity checks, not a traffic split plus a dashboard.
interviewImpact: Experiment design connects product metrics, rollout safety, interference, and decision limits.
solves: Determining whether a production change caused a product outcome.
useWhen: When randomization is ethical, feasible, and aligned with the decision.
tradeoff: Causal evidence costs traffic, time, operational complexity, and sometimes user exposure.
commonMistake: Saying A/B test it without unit, exposure, integrity, or safety constraints.
mechanism: Predeclare hypothesis, primary metric, guardrails, randomization unit, eligibility, exposure, ramp, duration, and stop rules.
Check assignment and sample-ratio mismatch before interpreting effects; examine interference and long-term limits.
alternatives: Use shadow or replay for technical validation without user impact.
Use quasi-experimental or staged observational evidence only with explicit causal limitations.
productConsequences: A valid experiment can reveal that offline gains do not improve user outcomes.
operationalConsequences: Assignment, exposure logging, isolation, guardrails, and ramp controls must remain reliable throughout the test.
failureModes: Sample-ratio mismatch invalidates the result.
Network effects violate independent treatment assumptions.
workedExample: Feed ranking randomizes by user, logs exposure, watches quality and latency guardrails, and ramps only after integrity checks.
Creator ecosystem effects are treated as an interference risk, not ignored.

exercise.prompt: Choose the randomization unit for a collaborative product where users interact with each other.
exercise.expected: Explain why user-level assignment may interfere and consider clusters, markets, or other designs with trade-offs.

interviewerProbes: What is the randomization and analysis unit?
How do you detect invalid assignment or interference?

levelOverlays.entry: State treatment, control, and one guardrail.
levelOverlays.mid: Add unit, exposure, SRM, ramp, and analysis integrity.
levelOverlays.senior: Handle interference, long-term effects, organizational overlap, and decision governance.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist deepens inference; SWE-ML owns trustworthy delivery and logging.

riskCallout: Do not experiment on unsafe or irreversible harm merely because randomization is technically possible.
decisionTrigger: What integrity or guardrail signal would stop the experiment before significance?

title: Monitoring, Drift & Performance Degradation
summary: Observe data, system, predictions, and delayed outcomes, then diagnose before retraining.
learningObjective: Separate drift signals from root cause and product impact.
scenario: CTR falls while feature null rate spikes, but the team automatically retrains for presumed model drift.
mentalModel: Drift is a symptom; diagnosis decides whether data, system, policy, model, or environment changed.
interviewImpact: Multi-layer monitoring supports safe alerts, diagnosis, rollback, and retraining policy.
solves: Detecting and explaining production degradation before delayed outcomes fully arrive.
useWhen: For every deployed learning or retrieval system.
tradeoff: Sensitive alerts catch issues early but create noise and operational load.
commonMistake: Monitoring only uptime or only a model metric.
mechanism: Monitor schema/missingness/freshness, errors/latency/saturation/cost, output distributions and slices, then delayed outcomes.
Link alerts to runbooks, version context, diagnosis, rollback, and evidence-driven retraining.
alternatives: Use representative sentinel evaluation when labels are too delayed for continuous measurement.
Use business process controls when a model metric cannot be observed reliably.
productConsequences: Outcome and slice monitoring reveal degradation that healthy infrastructure metrics miss.
operationalConsequences: Alert thresholds, ownership, dashboards, retention, and incident playbooks must be maintained.
failureModes: Every distribution change triggers retraining.
Delayed labels make a stale proxy look healthy.
workedExample: A feature null spike plus CTR drop points to data quality before model drift.
The response checks pipeline versions, falls back, repairs data, and only retrains if evidence supports it.

exercise.prompt: Diagnose simultaneous score shift, stable latency, rising nulls, and falling outcome quality.
exercise.expected: Investigate data/feature pipeline and version changes first; protect users with fallback before deciding to retrain.

interviewerProbes: Which signal is earliest and which proves outcome harm?
What action follows each alert?

levelOverlays.mid: Monitor four layers with runbooks.
levelOverlays.senior: Design ownership, regional/tenant slices, incident control, and evidence-driven policy.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML deepens telemetry; MLE connects outputs to delayed outcomes.

riskCallout: Monitor harmful errors and appeal outcomes where relevant, but minimize sensitive telemetry and access.
decisionTrigger: Which combination of signals distinguishes bad data from changed user behavior?

title: Feedback Loops, Exploration & Retraining
summary: Reason about how model actions alter future data and define evidence-driven update policies.
learningObjective: Identify endogenous labels and choose exploration and retraining triggers deliberately.
scenario: A recommender repeatedly exposes popular items, then treats their extra interactions as proof they are universally best.
mentalModel: The policy changes what becomes observable, so future data is partly produced by the model itself.
interviewImpact: Feedback loops connect exposure logging, exploration, evaluation, retraining, and ecosystem effects.
solves: Learning under selection and presentation bias created by prior decisions.
useWhen: When predictions determine exposure, enforcement, review, or resource allocation.
tradeoff: Exploration improves knowledge but can reduce short-term quality or increase risk.
commonMistake: Treating logged behavior as an unbiased sample or retraining on a calendar without validation.
mechanism: Trace policy to exposure, outcome, logging, dataset, retraining, and next policy.
Use bounded exploration, replay, correction, and schedule/event/performance triggers with acceptance gates.
alternatives: Use deterministic diversity or rotation when randomized exploration is unsafe.
Retrain only on validated change when frequent updates add instability.
productConsequences: Unchecked loops can narrow discovery, amplify popularity, or target repeatedly reviewed users.
operationalConsequences: Exploration allocation, replay datasets, trigger logic, and rollback require explicit ownership.
failureModes: The model learns only from its own exposures.
Frequent retraining amplifies a temporary logging incident.
workedExample: A recommender reserves bounded exploration for eligible underexposed items and logs propensity.
Retraining proceeds only after data quality and outcome checks pass.

exercise.prompt: Break a loop where the top-ranked creators receive nearly all future training signal.
exercise.expected: Add exposure-aware evaluation, bounded exploration or diversity policy, creator/user guardrails, and long-term monitoring.

interviewerProbes: How does your policy change future labels?
What evidence triggers retraining?

levelOverlays.mid: Add exploration and validated retraining triggers.
levelOverlays.senior: Model ecosystem incentives, adversarial adaptation, long-term effects, and governance.
levelOverlays.role: Applied Scientist studies bias correction; SWE-ML owns safe exploration and retraining systems.

riskCallout: Exploration must respect eligibility, safety, consent, and action reversibility; do not expose users to known harm for learning.
decisionTrigger: What evidence shows the current policy is narrowing the data it learns from?

title: Reliability & Graceful Degradation
summary: Keep decisions useful and safe when model, feature, index, data, or compute dependencies fail.
learningObjective: Design SLOs, timeouts, stale modes, fallbacks, load shedding, and recovery.
scenario: Neural reranking becomes a single point of failure for search even though lexical retrieval is healthy.
mentalModel: The safest useful fallback is part of the product, not an incident improvisation.
interviewImpact: Failure handling exposes dependency boundaries, action risk, and real production judgment.
solves: Maintaining bounded service and policy behavior during partial failure.
useWhen: For every production ML path, especially irreversible or high-harm actions.
tradeoff: Fallback simplicity and safety may reduce personalization or quality.
commonMistake: Treating the model or feature store as infallible and naming no stale-data policy.
mechanism: Set user-centered SLOs and bound each dependency with timeouts, budgets, isolation, and load shedding.
Define safe fallback, staleness limits, degraded observability, recovery, and disaster scenarios.
alternatives: Fail closed for unsafe actions and fail open only when policy explicitly allows it.
Serve a cached or deterministic baseline when personalization is unavailable.
productConsequences: Graceful degradation trades some quality for predictable availability and safety.
operationalConsequences: Fallbacks need capacity, compatibility, tests, alerts, and ownership like the primary path.
failureModes: The fallback depends on the same failed feature.
Stale predictions remain active past their safe horizon.
workedExample: Search skips neural reranking on timeout and returns permission-filtered lexical results.
The response marks degraded telemetry and limits stale index use.

exercise.prompt: Inject feature store, model, and index failures into a ranking path.
exercise.expected: Choose distinct bounded behavior for each dependency, preserve permissions, and name the user-visible consequence.

interviewerProbes: What is the fallback's own failure mode?
How stale is still safe?

levelOverlays.mid: Add SLOs, timeouts, isolation, and stale policy.
levelOverlays.senior: Cover regional failure, disaster recovery, multi-tenant isolation, and organizational ownership.
levelOverlays.role: SWE-ML deepens operational resilience; MLE ensures fallback quality remains valid.

riskCallout: For enforcement or financial actions, unavailable evidence should not silently become automatic punishment.
decisionTrigger: Which dependency failure requires a safe stop instead of a lower-quality fallback?

title: Responsible ML, Privacy, Security & Human Oversight
summary: Treat harm, privacy, abuse, auditability, review, and appeal as lifecycle design concerns.
learningObjective: Map concrete risks to preventive, detective, corrective, and human controls.
scenario: A moderation model directly punishes users with disputed labels, no appeal, and no audit trail.
mentalModel: The model estimates; policy, controls, and accountable people govern consequential action.
interviewImpact: Risk changes data access, objectives, thresholds, review capacity, logging, rollout, monitoring, and fallback.
solves: Systems that are technically effective but unsafe, unaccountable, invasive, or easy to abuse.
useWhen: Throughout the lifecycle, not as a final disclaimer.
tradeoff: Additional review and controls can add latency and cost but reduce preventable harm and improve reversibility.
commonMistake: Bolting on fairness at the end or making unsupported legal conclusions.
mechanism: Identify stakeholders, harms, sensitive data, abuse cases, disputed outcomes, and accountable owners.
Attach access, minimization, evaluation slices, review, appeal, audit, monitoring, and incident controls to the relevant lifecycle stage.
alternatives: Keep a human decision when evidence, reversibility, or accountability is insufficient for automation.
Use policy rules when learned behavior would be opaque or unstable for a high-impact boundary.
productConsequences: Human review and appeal can change both user trust and label quality.
operationalConsequences: Access reviews, audit trails, red-team tests, reviewer quality, and incident escalation need durable ownership.
failureModes: Sensitive attributes are used without a justified control purpose.
Appeals exist in policy but cannot correct data or future decisions.
workedExample: Moderation separates detection score, policy mapping, human review, enforcement, and appeal.
Reversals update audit state and future labels rather than disappearing into support notes.

exercise.prompt: Create a risk-and-control map for an automated account restriction.
exercise.expected: Include data minimization, subgroup errors, abuse, threshold policy, human review, notice, appeal, audit, and rollback.

interviewerProbes: Who can be harmed and how is the action reversed?
Which control prevents, detects, and corrects failure?

levelOverlays.entry: Name a relevant risk and one control.
levelOverlays.mid: Tie risk to data, threshold, review, and monitoring.
levelOverlays.senior: Resolve conflicting risks, auditability, policy evolution, ownership, and incident governance.
levelOverlays.role: Every role owns this boundary; depth shifts between modeling, platform controls, and product policy.

riskCallout: This material is engineering preparation, not legal or compliance advice; real deployments require domain and policy review.
decisionTrigger: What harm, uncertainty, or reversibility limit requires human oversight or no automation?
